sections.title: Welcome to the Filipino Bakery
sections.html:
Welcome to the Filipino Bakery

A Filipino bakery is more than a place that sells bread. It is the smell of pandesal before sunrise, the breadcrumb trail left by Spanish bread, the sweetness of coconut filling, and the familiar row of soft yellow cakes behind glass. These products carry traces of Spanish baking, American milling and cake making, Chinese pastry craft, local ingredients, and generations of Filipino adaptation.

This book turns that living tradition into practical formulas for the modern kitchen. Every recipe is written in grams first because a scale gives the most repeatable results. Approximate US measures are included for accessibility, but flour should never be packed into a cup. Finished-product photographs show the intended identity of each item. Four-stage procedure photographs show the critical transformations in mixing, shaping, filling, proofing, or finishing. The written cues tell you when the dough, filling, proof, and bake are actually ready.

The central lesson is simple: watch the dough, not only the clock. Temperature, flour strength, yeast freshness, humidity, and handling all change the schedule. Learn the physical cues and the bakery will become predictable.

sections.title: How to Use This Book
sections.html:
How to Use This Book

Read the entire recipe before mixing. Prepare fillings first when they must cool.

Use grams whenever possible. Place the mixing bowl on the scale and tare between ingredients.

Record room temperature, dough temperature, proof time, and bake time for every test batch.

Treat proofing times as ranges. The fingertip test and dough volume are more useful than a timer alone.

Let hot sugar, cheese, coconut, and custard fillings cool before tasting.

sections.title: Ingredients Equipment and Accuracy
sections.html:
Ingredients Equipment and Accuracy

Bread flour provides the gluten strength needed for soft rolls and enriched doughs. All-purpose flour is used where tenderness matters more than chew. Cake flour keeps mamon and pianono delicate. Instant yeast can be mixed directly with flour; if using active dry yeast, use the same weight and dissolve it in part of the warm liquid first.

sections.title: Dough Temperature Kneading and Fermentation
sections.html:
Dough Temperature Kneading and Fermentation

Aim for a finished dough temperature of 77 to 81°F / 25 to 27°C for most yeast breads in this book. If the room is warm, use cooler milk; if the room is cold, use warmer milk, but keep liquid below 110°F / 43°C so the yeast is not harmed.

A developed dough stretches into a thin translucent film before tearing. Enriched dough often looks rough at first; allow the flour to hydrate, then add butter gradually. Stop and scrape the bowl as needed. During bulk fermentation, cover the dough so its surface cannot dry. During final proof, a light fingertip indentation should return slowly. A quick rebound means more time is needed; a dent that collapses and remains may indicate overproofing.

sections.title: Procedure photographs
sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Mix flour, sugar, and yeast. Add milk and egg; mix until no dry flour remains. Rest 10 minutes.

3. Add salt and butter. Knead 8 to 12 minutes by mixer or 12 to 18 minutes by hand, until smooth and elastic.

4. Cover and bulk-ferment at 75 to 82°F / 24 to 28°C for 60 to 90 minutes, until about doubled.

5. Gently deflate. Divide into 20 equal pieces. Round each tightly, keeping the seam underneath.

6. Roll every piece in fine breadcrumbs and arrange on parchment, about 1½ inches apart.

7. Cover and proof 40 to 60 minutes. A light fingertip dent should return slowly.

8. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until pale golden, 190 to 195°F / 88 to 91°C inside. Cool on a rack.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The dough is tacky but manageable and passes a thin windowpane test. The baked crumb pulls into fine, moist strands.

Storage and serving

Bag when barely warm. Keep 2 days at room temperature or freeze up to 1 month. Rewarm 5 minutes at 300°F.

Troubleshooting

Dense rolls: proof longer. Dry rolls: weigh flour and shorten baking. Flat rolls: avoid overproofing.

sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Make and knead the enriched dough as for pandesal. Bulk-ferment until doubled.

3. For the filling, melt 80 g butter over low heat. Stir in brown sugar, 60 g crumbs, 40 g milk, vanilla, and a pinch of salt for 2 to 3 minutes. Cool completely.

4. Divide dough into 16 pieces. Round, cover, and rest 12 minutes.

5. Roll each piece into a 6- to 7-inch tapered oval. Spread 15 to 18 g filling, leaving a border.

6. Roll from the wide end toward the narrow end. Pinch the seam closed.

7. Brush lightly with milk, coat with crumbs, and place seam-side down.

8. Proof 40 to 55 minutes. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until light golden. Cool at least 10 minutes before eating.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The filling is a cool, spreadable paste, never runny. Properly rolled bread has a visible spiral and no leaking seam.

Storage and serving

Store airtight 2 days. Freeze wrapped rolls up to 1 month.

Troubleshooting

Leaking: cool filling and leave a border. Dry center: do not overcook filling. Unrolling: pinch seam and bake seam-side down.

sections.title: Procedure photographs
sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 340°F / 170°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Mix flour, sugar, yeast, milk, eggs, and yolk. Rest 10 minutes. Add salt, then knead in 100 g butter gradually.

3. Knead to a strong windowpane; enriched dough may need 12 to 15 minutes by mixer.

4. Bulk-ferment 75 to 100 minutes, until doubled. Divide into 12 pieces and rest 10 minutes.

5. Roll each into a 14-inch rope. Coil loosely in greased ensaymada molds, leaving room to expand.

6. Proof 50 to 75 minutes until very puffy and the coils nearly meet.

7. Bake 16 to 20 minutes. Do not deeply brown. Cool fully.

8. Beat topping butter until creamy. Spread lightly over each bread; dust with sugar and finish with grated cheese.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The dough feels satiny, extensible, and rich. The finished crumb is feathery rather than cakey.

Storage and serving

Refrigerate topped bread up to 3 days; bring to room temperature before serving. Freeze untopped bread.

Troubleshooting

Greasy dough: butter was added too fast. Tight crumb: knead and proof fully. Dry bread: reduce bake time.

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Prepare and bulk-ferment the dough using the pandesal mixing method.

3. Simmer coconut, brown sugar, water, vanilla, and a pinch of salt for 8 to 12 minutes until glossy and nearly dry. Cool fully.

4. Divide dough into 16 pieces; round and rest 10 minutes.

5. Flatten each into a 4-inch disk. Place 25 g filling in the center. Gather edges and pinch firmly.

6. Set seam-side down, then flatten gently. Optional: make two shallow decorative slashes.

7. Proof 40 to 60 minutes. Brush with milk or egg wash.

8. Bake 16 to 20 minutes until evenly golden. Cool before opening.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The filling clumps together without free syrup. The sealed bun feels taut with no thin spots.

Storage and serving

Room temperature 2 days; refrigerate up to 4 days and rewarm.

Troubleshooting

Burst buns: filling too wet or seal too thin. Hollow pocket: flatten the filling and remove trapped air.

sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Combine dry ingredients; add milk and egg. Rest 10 minutes. Knead in salt and butter until smooth.

3. Bulk-ferment 60 to 80 minutes; monay dough need not become as airy as pandesal.

4. Divide into 12 pieces of about 78 g. Shape into tight ovals.

5. Arrange on parchment and proof 35 to 50 minutes, only until about 75 percent larger.

6. With a greased bench scraper, press a deep lengthwise groove nearly halfway through each oval.

7. Brush with milk. Bake 18 to 22 minutes until medium golden.

8. Cool under a light clean towel for a softer crust.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The crumb is close and substantial but not heavy. The center split remains clearly visible after baking.

Storage and serving

Keep airtight 2 days; slice and toast after that.

Troubleshooting

Split disappears: groove was too shallow or proof too long. Heavy bread: insufficient kneading or proofing.

sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 360°F / 182°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Mix and knead to a firm, smooth dough. Bulk-ferment 50 to 70 minutes.

3. Divide into 14 pieces, about 65 g each. Round very tightly.

4. Proof 25 to 40 minutes; putok is deliberately underproofed compared with pandesal.

5. Using clean kitchen scissors, snip a deep cross in each top, creating four points.

6. Mist or brush lightly with water and press sugar onto the cut tops.

7. Bake 16 to 20 minutes until the peaks are well browned and the sides are golden.

8. Cool fully; the exterior firms as it cools.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

A proper putok has a dramatic burst top and a compact, pleasantly chewy crumb.

Storage and serving

Airtight 2 days. Reheat briefly to refresh.

Troubleshooting

No burst: dough overproofed. Dense raw line: pieces too large or bake too short.

Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Prepare enriched dough and bulk-ferment until doubled.

3. Mix topping butter, sugar, grated cheese, and crumbs into a soft paste.

4. Divide dough into 16 pieces. Flatten each; enclose a 7 to 8 g cheese cube and seal.

5. Shape into short ovals and place seam-side down.

6. Proof 40 to 55 minutes. Spread a thin strip of topping down each roll.

7. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until golden and fragrant.

8. Cool 10 minutes before serving so the cheese is not dangerously hot.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The topping stays on the roll and becomes lightly crisp while the bread remains soft.

Storage and serving

Room temperature 1 day or refrigerate up to 3 days. Rewarm before serving.

Troubleshooting

Escaping cheese: use firm cheese and seal well. Burned topping: tent loosely for final minutes.

Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Prepare dough and allow the first rise.

3. Cook filling ingredients except coloring over medium-low heat, stirring, until thick and moldable, 5 to 8 minutes. Tint red sparingly. Cool completely.

4. Divide dough into 16 pieces and rest 10 minutes.

5. Roll each into a rectangle. Place a compact 25 g strip of filling along one side.

6. Fold or roll over the filling, seal all edges, and shape into a neat oblong.

7. Proof 40 to 55 minutes and brush with egg wash.

8. Bake 16 to 19 minutes until golden. Cool before slicing.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The filling is moist and cohesive, not wet. The red center forms a clean bar inside the bread.

Storage and serving

Airtight 2 days or refrigerated 4 days.

Troubleshooting

Gummy filling: cook longer. Split bread: cool filling and avoid overfilling.

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Make and bulk-ferment the dough. Chill very soft ube halaya until scoopable.

3. Divide dough into 16 portions. Round and rest 10 minutes.

4. Flatten each into a disk and place 25 g ube in the center.

5. Gather edges, expel excess air, and pinch securely. Shape round or oval.

6. Lightly brush with milk and coat with breadcrumbs.

7. Proof 40 to 55 minutes. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until light golden.

8. Cool at least 15 minutes to allow the filling to settle.

sections.title: What success looks like

Thick halaya holds its shape on a spoon. The baked filling remains creamy without soaking the crumb.

Storage and serving

Room temperature 1 day; refrigerate 4 days or freeze 1 month.

Troubleshooting

Leaks: use thicker, colder halaya. Pale bottom: use a light metal pan preheated with the oven.

Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Mix and knead all ingredients, adding butter after the initial 10-minute rest. Develop a strong windowpane.

3. Bulk-ferment 60 to 90 minutes. Grease two loaf pans.

4. Divide dough in half. For each loaf, divide into three, round, and rest 10 minutes.

5. Flatten each piece into a rectangle, roll tightly, and place three rolls seam-side down in each pan.

6. Proof until the center rises about 1 inch over the rim, 50 to 80 minutes.

7. Bake 28 to 34 minutes to an internal temperature of 195°F / 91°C.

8. Unmold immediately and cool completely before slicing.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The loaf slices cleanly into a fine, even crumb with no large tunnels.

Storage and serving

Bag only when fully cool. Room temperature 3 days or freeze sliced.

Troubleshooting

Collapsed sides: bake fully and unmold promptly. Large holes: press out large gas bubbles during shaping.

sections.html:
Procedure photographs

Key procedure stages shown from left to right

Method

1. Before frying, bring the oil to 340 to 350°F / 171 to 177°C. Monitor it continuously with a thermometer.

2. Prepare dough and bulk-ferment until doubled.

3. Divide into 16 pieces. Roll each into a 10-inch rope, fold in half, and twist. Pinch the ends.

4. Place on small parchment squares. Proof 30 to 45 minutes until puffy.

5. Heat 2 to 3 inches of oil in a heavy pot. Keep a lid nearby, never fill beyond halfway, and do not leave oil unattended.

6. Lower pieces carefully, removing parchment with tongs. Fry 60 to 90 seconds per side until deep golden.

7. Drain briefly on a rack or paper towels.

8. While warm, roll in sugar. Cool slightly before eating.

sections.title: What success looks like
sections.html:
What success looks like

The oil bubbles steadily but not violently. The center is fully cooked and light, without an oily line.

Storage and serving

Best the day made. Rewarm uncoated pieces in an oven, then recoat.

Troubleshooting

Greasy bread: oil too cool or dough overproofed. Dark outside/raw center: oil too hot.

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F / 175°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Line a 10 by 15 inch jelly-roll pan. Whisk yolks with 40 g sugar, milk, oil, and vanilla; fold in sifted flour and baking powder.

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. After the first 15 minutes of baking, reduce it to 325°F / 163°C as directed.

Method

1. Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Position a rack near the center unless the recipe states otherwise.

2. Cook mashed mung beans with sugar, oil, and a pinch of salt over low heat until a firm paste forms. Cool; divide into 20 balls.

3. For water dough, mix 250 g flour, sugar, salt, water, and oil; knead smooth. Rest 20 minutes.

4. For oil dough, mix 140 g flour and shortening into a paste. Divide both doughs into 20 portions.

5. Wrap each oil-dough piece inside water dough. Roll into an oval, coil, turn 90 degrees, roll again, and coil. Rest 10 minutes.

6. Flatten each coil, enclose mung bean filling, seal, and press into a 2½-inch disk.

7. Place seam-side down. Brush with egg wash and prick once.

8. Bake 20 to 25 minutes until golden and flaky.

Leaking: filling too moist. Tough layers: overwork the laminated dough.

sections.title: Commercial Scaling and Production
sections.html:
Commercial Scaling and Production

A bakery formula becomes scalable when every ingredient is expressed as a percentage of total flour weight. Flour always equals 100 percent. To find an ingredient percentage, divide its weight by flour weight and multiply by 100. To scale, multiply the desired flour weight by each percentage.

For 100 pandesal at 46 g each, allow about 4.6 kg total dough plus normal handling loss. The base recipe produces roughly 940 g before breadcrumb coating, so multiply the formula by approximately 4.9. Make a test batch in the actual mixer before committing to production; large mixers develop heat and gluten differently.

sections.title: Suggested Production Order
sections.html:
Suggested Production Order

1. Prepare long-cooking fillings and cool them rapidly in shallow pans.

2. Scale ingredients into clearly labeled containers.

3. Mix leanest dough first and richest dough last.

4. Bulk-ferment in covered, food-safe containers marked with the start time.

5. Divide by weight, shape, fill, and place on labeled trays.

6. Proof by product readiness rather than loading every tray at once.

7. Bake pale breads before strongly flavored or high-sugar products when practical.

8. Cool to room temperature before bagging. Record yield and waste.

sections.title: Food Safety and Allergen Control
sections.html:
Food Safety and Allergen Control

The recipes commonly contain wheat, milk, eggs, sesame, and coconut. Some cheeses and fillings may contain additional allergens. Prevent cross-contact, sanitize work surfaces, use separate utensils where needed, and label products accurately. Refrigerate custard, dairy-rich toppings, and perishable fillings at 40°F / 4°C or below. Cool cooked fillings promptly. Follow applicable local health, labeling, and cottage-food regulations before selling.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
Glossary

Bulk fermentation. The first rise after mixing and before dividing.

Degas. To press out large fermentation bubbles without crushing all the air.

Final proof. The last rise after shaping and before baking or frying.

Hydration. Liquid as a percentage of flour weight.

Mise en place. All ingredients measured and equipment prepared before work begins.

Seam side. The joined edge created when dough is rolled or closed.

Tangzhong. A cooked flour-and-liquid paste used to improve softness and shelf life.

Windowpane. A thin sheet of stretched dough that shows adequate gluten development.

Publishing Package

Recommended Subtitle

Authentic Panaderya Breads Pastries and Cakes with Exact Measurements and Step by Step Methods

Book Description

Bring the warmth of a Filipino neighborhood bakery into your own kitchen. The Filipino Bakery Book presents reliable, clearly written recipes for pandesal, Spanish bread, ensaymada, pan de coco, monay, putok, cheese bread, kalihim, ube bread, mamon, pianono, egg pie, hopia, and more. Every formula includes weights in grams, approximate US measures, temperature targets, shaping instructions, visual doneness cues, storage guidance, and practical troubleshooting. Whether you are rediscovering breads from childhood, teaching the next generation, or testing products for a small bakery, this collection gives you the structure to bake with confidence and consistency.
